newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysia's Country Heights transforms tin mine.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia's Country Heights transforms tin mine.

text.p: Malaysian property developer Country Heights Holdings Bhd hopes its alchemy will turn an old tin mine into gold.

The company headed by Lee Kim Yew is converting a disused tin mine into a luxury resort, complete with million dollar homes and a golf course that offers a Boeing 737 airliner to fly in its members for golfing jaunts.

After starting as little more than a concept eight years ago, the Mines Resort City, located about 20 km (13 miles) south of Kuala Lumpur, has transformed 1,000 acres (405 hectares) of what used to be the world's largest open-cast tin mine.
The mine's landscape has been replaced by sprawling bungalows in various states of construction, an 18-hole golf course and a shopping centre with a canal running through it.
When the project began in 1989, Malaysia was reeling from a recession that began two years earlier. "Yes, a lot (of people) were sceptical," Lee said in an interview.
"We believed we had a concept and we thought we could push it through," said Lee, the firm's managing director.

But the key to success, Lee said, was not to be fixed on preconceived ideas. For instance, the company had first envisioned placing the homes at the edge of the former mining lake. But they later had second thoughts based on possible changes in the lakeshore land.
After conducting soil tests, the company decided to put the golf course by the lake. The buildings were constructed on land found to be underlaid with granite, he said.
Country Heights expects its Mines projects, including its Palace of the Golden Horses theme hotel, to be completed this year.

For the six months ended August 31, 1996, the company reported net profit of 42.0 million ringgit ($16.8 million) against 26.01 million in the corresponding period. Its turnover jumped to 152.20 million from 76.19 million in that half-year.
The firm has said it aims to boost pretax profits by about 20 percent per year over the next three years. For the six months to August, its pretax profit was 63.07 million ringgit.
Lee is still optimistic about the company's results, despite a recent central bank ruling that tightened restrictions on bank loans for property to 20 percent of total loans outstanding.
"We will do better," he said, without elaborating, when asked about results for 1997. "I think those that will be affected are those (companies) that depend on high gearing."
In fact, Lee said he welcomed Bank Negara Malaysia's intervention to stave off a potential property bubble.
The central bank's measures were "trying to build a more healthy economy that grows steadily rather than getting it very, very heated up", Lee said.

Lee is also casting his vision towards the company's 500 million ringgit Borneo Highland Resort on the island of Borneo, where Country Heights aims to do in a rainforest what it is doing on an abandoned tin mine. ($1=2.5 ringgit)
